h1: New York HOA Lien and Foreclosure Threat Response Demand Letter
metaTitle: NY HOA Lien Foreclosure Demand Letter Generator
metaDescription: Respond to New York HOA lien filings and foreclosure threats with a state-specific demand letter. Protect your home rights under NY Real Property Law today.
statuteCitation: N.Y. Real Property Law § 339-z and § 339-aa (Condominium Act); N.Y. Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law (RPAPL) Article 13
deadline: Condominium foreclosure requires at least 90 days' written notice before the action is commenced (RPL § 339-aa); the recorded lien lasts six years from filing
penalty: A lien that includes unauthorized charges can be challenged; on payment the unit owner is entitled to an instrument certifying payment (RPL § 339-aa); the FDCPA provides damages if a debt collector violated it
introParagraph: If your New York HOA or condominium association has filed a lien against your property or threatened foreclosure, you have important rights under state law. New York treats HOA and condo liens differently than mortgages, and associations must follow strict procedural requirements before they can enforce a lien or initiate foreclosure. Many liens contain errors, include improper late fees, or were filed without proper notice. A well-drafted demand letter can force the HOA to validate the debt, correct improper charges, or withdraw an invalid lien before the dispute escalates to court. Acting quickly is critical because lien priority and foreclosure timelines move fast in New York, and missing deadlines can put your home at serious risk.
lawExplanation:
New York condominium associations derive lien rights from the Condominium Act, N.Y. Real Property Law § 339-z, which gives the board of managers a lien on each unit for unpaid common charges and interest, and under § 339-aa the lien is effective from the filing of a verified notice of lien in the office of the recording officer where the declaration is filed and continues until paid or six years from filing. Under § 339-aa, the lien may be foreclosed by suit in the board's name in like manner as a mortgage under RPAPL Article 13, but the board must give the owner at least 90 days' written notice, in fourteen-point type, stating the amount due, before commencing the foreclosure. Homeowner associations (HOAs) governing single-family communities typically derive lien rights from their recorded Declaration of Covenants, Conditions, and Restrictions (CC&Rs), enforced under common law and the specific terms of those documents.

Key protections for New York owners include: (1) the lien must accurately state the amount due, including only assessments authorized by the declaration and bylaws; (2) the condominium lien is prior to all other liens except tax liens, sums unpaid on a first mortgage of record, and certain subordinate government-agency mortgages (RPL § 339-z); (3) the 90-day foreclosure notice in RPL § 339-aa must be given before suit; and (4) if the HOA or its agent is a third-party debt collector, the federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) and New York General Business Law Article 29-H (§ 600 et seq.) may impose validation and anti-harassment requirements.

New York courts have repeatedly invalidated HOA liens that include unauthorized fines, excessive late fees, or attorney's fees not permitted by the governing documents. Owners may also challenge liens that fail to credit payments correctly or that were filed without the board action required by the bylaws. On payment of the unpaid sums secured by the lien, the unit owner is entitled to an instrument duly executed and acknowledged certifying payment (RPL § 339-aa).
letterStrategy:
A demand letter is often the fastest and least expensive way to resolve a New York HOA lien dispute. The letter should be sent by certified mail, return receipt requested, to both the association and its managing agent or attorney. It should formally dispute the debt, demand a full itemized accounting of every charge included in the lien (assessments, late fees, interest, fines, and legal fees), and cite the specific provisions of the declaration, bylaws, and N.Y. Real Property Law §§ 339-z and 339-aa that govern the association's authority.

An effective letter accomplishes several things at once: it triggers the HOA's obligation to validate the debt under the FDCPA if a collector is involved; it creates a documented record showing the homeowner attempted resolution in good faith, which courts view favorably; it puts the board on notice that improper charges must be removed; and it warns that continued enforcement of an invalid lien may result in counterclaims for slander of title, wrongful lien filing, and attorney's fees. The letter should also demand that any satisfied or improperly inflated lien be corrected or released and a certificate of payment issued (RPL § 339-aa).

Many New York associations back down or negotiate when faced with a detailed, statute-citing demand letter, particularly if foreclosure litigation would expose board decisions and accounting practices to discovery. If the HOA refuses to respond or proceeds with foreclosure, the letter becomes important evidence supporting bad-faith claims and fee-shifting in subsequent litigation. Including a specific deadline for response—typically 14 to 30 days—keeps pressure on the association to act before the dispute escalates.
proceduralNotes: New York small claims courts have a $10,000 limit ($5,000 in town and village courts) and generally cannot adjudicate title or order lien discharge—those claims belong in Supreme Court. Foreclosure actions are filed in Supreme Court. Filing fees in Supreme Court typically run $210 for the index number plus motion fees. A recorded condominium lien continues for six years from filing (RPL § 339-aa), and actions on a contractual obligation are generally subject to a six-year limitation (CPLR § 213). Homeowners facing foreclosure may qualify for free legal help through court-sponsored foreclosure programs.

faq.q: Can a New York HOA really foreclose on my home for unpaid dues?
faq.a: Yes. Under N.Y. Real Property Law § 339-aa, a condominium board can foreclose a recorded lien for unpaid common charges by suit in like manner as a mortgage, after giving the owner at least 90 days' written notice stating the amount due. HOAs in planned communities can foreclose if their declaration grants that right. However, the association must strictly follow procedural requirements, including proper lien filing and notice. Many liens contain defects that can be challenged before foreclosure proceeds.

faq.q: What charges can an HOA legally include in a New York lien?
faq.a: An HOA can only include amounts authorized by the recorded declaration, bylaws, and New York law. This typically covers unpaid assessments, reasonable late fees, and interest at the rate specified in the governing documents. Fines for rule violations are often disputed and may not be lienable unless expressly authorized. Attorney's fees are recoverable only if the declaration or statute permits. Always demand a written itemization to identify improper charges.

faq.q: How long do I have to respond to an HOA lien notice in New York?
faq.a: Deadlines vary based on your governing documents and whether a foreclosure has been filed. For a condominium lien, the board must give at least 90 days' written notice before commencing foreclosure (RPL § 339-aa). If you've been served with a foreclosure summons and complaint, the time to answer is stated in the summons, so check it immediately. Sending a demand letter immediately preserves your rights and may delay or prevent court action.

faq.q: Does the FDCPA apply to New York HOA collection efforts?
faq.a: The federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act applies when a third-party debt collector or law firm collects HOA debts on behalf of the association. It does not typically cover the association itself collecting in-house. When applicable, the FDCPA requires written validation of the debt, prohibits harassment, and allows damages up to $1,000 plus attorney's fees for violations. New York's General Business Law Article 29-H (§ 600 et seq.) regulates debt collection practices.

faq.q: Can I recover damages if my New York HOA filed an improper lien?
faq.a: Possibly. Owners may bring claims such as slander of title or breach of fiduciary duty against board members in some circumstances, and may be entitled to an instrument certifying payment once the lien is paid (RPL § 339-aa). If FDCPA violations occurred, statutory damages and fee-shifting are available in federal or state court.
